items.item: The gap between a run's logical date and its actual execution time isn't a quirk of display — it's why a daily run 'for' January first can safely read data up to but not including January second, and why manually triggered runs (not on the schedule) don't get a meaningful data_interval unless explicitly given one.

at.step: Reveal: logical date vs data interval, measured

items.item: Catchup being off by default in Airflow 3 is a behaviour every Dag author inherits silently: a Dag paused for two weeks and re-enabled with catchup=False will not 'catch up' on those two weeks at all, only schedule the latest interval going forward — a common surprise for anyone expecting Airflow 2's older defaults.

at.step: Reveal: catchup, off by default, measured

items.item: Backfill's max_active_runs and the Dag's own max_active_runs are genuinely two separate knobs — a Dag configured for high normal-operation concurrency can still have its backfills throttled tighter (or looser) without touching its day-to-day scheduling behaviour at all.

at.step: Reveal: bounded concurrency, run for real

items.item: This topic's own kill-and-resume demo is the concrete proof that 'resumable' means something specific and verifiable: not just that the backfill eventually finishes, but that the six already-successful runs kept their original start_date timestamps across the restart — direct evidence they were never re-executed, not just re-marked.

at.step: Reveal: kill it, restart it, measured

items.item: Dagster's per-partition-vs-single-run choice is a real engineering trade, not a cosmetic one: single-run backfills only work when the asset's own code already operates on a partition_time_window or partition_key_range rather than one partition_key at a time — switching to single_run without rewriting that code silently breaks the asset.

at.step: Reveal: Dagster's other shape

items.item: The blast-radius calculation generalizes past this topic's own numbers: any backfill's cost on a shared source is (requests per unit of history) times (how much history), compared against that source's own sustained budget — the same arithmetic applies whether the unit is a day, an hour, or a single API page.

at.step: Predict: does a backfill get its own budget?

items.item: A reader who only remembers 'backfills are bounded and resumable' may assume that makes them safe by default — this topic's recap deliberately keeps the blast-radius finding in the same breath, because bounded concurrency protects the scheduler's own state, not the request budget of whatever the backfill reads from.

The reprocess-behaviour predict step (none/failed/completed) matters most exactly when a backfill is re-run after partially succeeding — picking 'completed' by habit when 'none' was intended will silently redo already-correct work, the opposite failure mode from the one the hook warns about.

at.step: Prove it

items.item: Airflow's auto-detection of a partitioned Dag's timetable (CronPartitionTimetable) means the exact same --from-date/--to-date CLI invocation behaves differently depending on the Dag's own timetable type — a detail easy to miss when copying a backfill command between a plain cron-scheduled Dag and a partitioned one.

This topic's logical-date and catchup measurements both call Airflow's CronDataIntervalTimetable directly rather than running a full scheduler cycle — a deliberate scope choice that isolates the timetable's own scheduling logic from the scheduler process's unrelated mechanics, which the backfill experiment (reveal 5 and 6) exercises instead.

'Resumable' in this topic's sense is distinct from the idempotency property topic 2 taught: idempotency makes a single re-run of one task harmless, while resumability here is about the orchestrator's own bookkeeping correctly skipping work it already knows is done — a backfill can be resumable even for tasks that aren't perfectly idempotent, as long as the orchestrator never re-queues the ones that finished.
